title: Indian Professionals Turn to O-1 'Einstein' Visa as H-1B Lottery Frustrations Mount
excerpt: With Indian O-1 approvals nearly tripling in three years and USCIS expanding qualifying fields to include AI, more tech workers are choosing merit over lottery luck.
body:
• Indian O-1 visa approvals surged from 487 in 2020 to 1,418 in 2023, with USCIS now recognizing AI and quantum computing as qualifying extraordinary-ability fields.
  • The O-1 visa has no annual cap or lottery and carries approval rates between 93.9% and 94.6%, far above H-1B selection odds.
  • A January 2025 USCIS policy update expanded eligibility for startup founders and broadened the types of evidence accepted.
  • Total filing costs typically range from $10,000 to $30,000, but professionals see the visa as a more controllable path than the H-1B lottery.

For three consecutive years, Tanush Sharanarthi entered the H-1B lottery. Three times, his name was not selected. The 26-year-old Bengaluru-born AI specialist, now working at IBM in California, decided to try a different route entirely — and won approval for the O-1 visa, reserved for individuals with "extraordinary ability."

"From three years of striking out in the H-1B lottery to finally being approved for the O-1 'Einstein' visa in the field of Artificial Intelligence. I played the H-1B game of chance. Three tickets, three misses. Turns out, consistency pays better than lottery."

— Tanush Sharanarthi, AI specialist at IBM

Sharanarthi is far from alone. Data from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services shows Indian O-1 approvals climbed from 487 in 2020 to 1,418 in 2023 — a nearly threefold increase. India now ranks among the top three source countries for O-1 petitions, behind only the United Kingdom and China, according to VisaVerge.

Why the Shift Is Accelerating

The H-1B visa, long the default work visa for Indian tech professionals, has become increasingly unpredictable. A lottery-based selection system means even highly qualified candidates can be rejected purely by chance, year after year. New fee structures, including a $100,000 surcharge for certain offshore petitions, have added further barriers.

The O-1 visa operates on an entirely different model. There is no annual cap, no lottery, and no degree requirement. USCIS processed 31,681 O-1 petitions in FY 2025 with approval rates between 93.9% and 94.6% — significantly higher odds than the H-1B lottery offers.

A policy update issued by USCIS on January 8, 2025, broadened the visa's reach further. The agency formally recognized AI, machine learning, and quantum computing as fields where extraordinary ability can be demonstrated. It also expanded eligibility for startup founders, allowing applicants to petition through companies they own if the business is active and supported by contracts or other documentation.

How Applicants Qualify

The O-1A visa, which covers science, technology, business, and education, requires applicants to demonstrate sustained national or international recognition. Candidates must meet at least three of eight criteria established by USCIS, including awards, published media coverage, patents or original contributions, memberships in elite associations, and high salary relative to peers.

Indian applicants typically build cases combining funding records, expert recommendation letters, press coverage, patents, and leadership roles. The 2025 policy update widened acceptable evidence to include online features, conference invitations, and early-career awards — changes that help rising professionals who have strong market credentials but are not yet household names.

The Cost Equation

The base filing fee for Form I-129 is $460, with an additional $2,805 for premium processing that guarantees a decision within 15 days. However, most applicants spend between $10,000 and $30,000 once attorney fees and document preparation are included, according to VisaVerge.

For many, the expense is justified by the control it offers. Unlike the H-1B lottery, where selection is random regardless of qualifications, the O-1 rewards a documented track record. Initial approvals last up to three years, with unlimited one- or three-year extensions available as long as the qualifying work continues.

A Broader Trend

Sharanarthi's story echoes a growing pattern. Companies including Tesla, Microsoft, McKinsey, and Google have expanded their use of O-1 sponsorship for Indian talent, according to USCIS data cited by VisaVerge. Many O-1 holders later use their evidence portfolios to pursue EB-1A green cards, creating a clearer long-term immigration pathway.

The trend reflects a fundamental tension in U.S. immigration policy: a system that subjects many of its most qualified applicants to a lottery while offering a merit-based alternative that relatively few know about or pursue. As H-1B becomes harder to rely on, the O-1 is emerging as the path of choice for Indian professionals willing to invest the time to build their case.
nri_angle: Indian tech professionals are increasingly turning to the O-1 visa as a merit-based alternative after repeated H-1B lottery rejections, with approvals nearly tripling in three years.
author: Diaspora Desk
